Give each number its source population: SURMOUNT-1 weight averages are for adults without diabetes, Zepbound pooled GI rates per dose vs placebo, Mounjaro rates only if they're labelled as type 2 diabetes trials. Give one approximate month-1 weight average with placebo alongside, or describe only the curve's shape. Organise the timeline by experience ('first days', 'first weeks', 'when your prescriber increases the dose'), never by a dosing calendar. Birth control: the label says it 'may reduce the efficacy' of birth control pills for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase, so ask your prescriber about backup options. Keep the rest of the plan as written.

plan.why: The owner's top-priority broad search question. Broad Lane A videos earned 233–1,009 min while narrow ones earned 7–85, and New Year starters arrive in about 6 weeks. | fact-check: Good choice: it's a broad, searched Lane A question that the playbook lists as a priority, and the plan already avoids dosing. The label's gastric-emptying wording ('the delay is largest after the first dose and diminishes over time') is real. So is the oral-contraceptive note for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase. Four things to tighten. (a) Population scope: the title says Mounjaro, but SURMOUNT-1 weight figures apply only to adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without type 2 diabetes. Mounjaro-label side-effect rates come from type 2 diabetes trials. Each number must name its label and population. Don't mix them. (b) First-month weight: in the first 4 weeks of SURMOUNT-1, every tirzepatide arm was still on the starting dose. So a per-arm month-1 figure means nothing, and saying why would reveal the schedule. Give one approximate figure off the curve: 'about', 'on average', 'averages, not predictions', with the placebo arm alongside. If the curve can't be read reliably from the NEJM figure, drop the number and describe the shape. (c) A 'week by week' timeline must not imply a dosing schedule. Don't say 'week 4 is when your dose goes up'. Use only 'your prescriber increases it gradually'. (d) Birth control chapter: quote the label's 'may reduce the efficacy' wording. Its advice to switch to a non-oral method or add a barrier method goes as 'the label advises; ask your prescriber which option fits you'. Don't make it a personal instruction. Warning-signs chapter: the pancreatitis card keeps 'right away', and the scoped don't-stop line comes after the emergency cards. For dehydration and kidney, keep to the label's wording about GI fluid loss. The low-blood-sugar line names insulin or a sulfonylurea. Gallbladder symptoms are optional, label wording only.

package.description:
Starting tirzepatide (Mounjaro or Zepbound)? Here's what the first month can look like, based on the FDA labels and trial data.

In Zepbound's weight-management trials, nausea was reported by 25–29% on tirzepatide (depending on dose) vs 8% on placebo, and most nausea, vomiting and diarrhea reports came during dose escalation. Mounjaro's US label uses type 2 diabetes trials, so ask your prescriber which figures apply to you.

Safety: Severe stomach-area pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting (possible pancreatitis): stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. Swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing (possible serious allergic reaction): stop using it and call your local emergency number or get medical help right away. If you can't keep fluids down, contact your prescriber. Low blood sugar risk may be higher if you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea. On birth control pills? The label says tirzepatide may reduce their efficacy for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase, so ask your prescriber about backup options.

script.hook_pattern: Visceral 'you' question with an instant answer: sentence 1 names tirzepatide and the viewer's first-month worry, the short answer comes by about 12 s, a second concrete number (nausea rates vs placebo) lands at 15–30 s, then a one-sentence open loop (the first-dose detail) that pays off in the birth control chapter

scenes.narration: Starting tirzepatide and wondering what your first month on Mounjaro or Zepbound will feel like?
scenes.retention_device: Direct question that matches the title, so viewers know they're in the right video

scenes.narration: Short answer. Tirzepatide turns appetite down. Stomach side effects are common, and they mostly show up around dose increases. And the scale moves gradually, not overnight.

items: Stomach effects cluster at dose increases

scenes.retention_device: Short answer delivered by about 12 s

scenes.narration: Here's one number to hold onto. In Zepbound's weight-management trials, nausea was reported by twenty-five to twenty-nine percent of people on tirzepatide, depending on dose. On placebo, eight percent.
scenes.retention_device: Second concrete payoff at 15–30 s, where most curves drop

scenes.narration: In the main obesity trial, stomach side effects were mostly mild to moderate, and happened mainly while the dose was being stepped up.
scenes.retention_device: Reassurance that eases the tension from the stat

scenes.narration: There's also one detail about your very first dose that the label spells out, and it matters if you take birth control pills.

visual.stock_query: closed label with glowing question mark

scenes.retention_device: One-sentence open loop that pays off in the birth control chapter

scenes.narration: Imagine someone called Rosa. She's fifty-one and has just been prescribed tirzepatide. The carton is sitting on her kitchen counter. She's hopeful, and honestly, a bit nervous.

visual.stock_query: hopeful nervous woman kitchen counter carton

scenes.narration: If that's you, the nerves make sense. So let's swap the scary stories for what the label and the trials actually show.

visual.stock_query: phone rumors swapped for open book

scenes.retention_device: Names the feeling and validates it before the first chapter

scenes.narration: So what's actually going on in your body in those first few days?

visual.stock_query: sunrise calendar first days title card

scenes.retention_device: Chapter opens with a question, not background

scenes.narration: Tirzepatide acts on two gut-hormone receptors, GIP and GLP-1.

visual.stock_query: two friendly keys fitting two locks

scenes.narration: And the label says it decreases calorie intake, likely through its effects on appetite.
scenes.retention_device: Label-backed explanation of the felt change

scenes.narration: Some people describe this as the food noise going quieter. Fewer of those ten p.m. pulls toward the fridge.

visual.stock_query: person at night fridge, calm expression

scenes.narration: If you've ever felt that pull was purely a willpower problem, you're not alone. Appetite is shaped by hormones too.

visual.stock_query: relieved person, weight lifted off shoulders

scenes.narration: How strongly people notice it varies, so jot down what you notice for your prescriber.
scenes.retention_device: Gives the viewer a small action, which builds agency

scenes.narration: There's a second effect. Tirzepatide slows how quickly your stomach empties, so food stays there longer.

visual.stock_query: cartoon stomach with slow traffic light

scenes.narration: So here's your first practical step. In those first days, try smaller portions, eat slowly, and stop at the first sign of fullness.
scenes.retention_device: Practical payoff before chapter 1 ends (about 70 s)

scenes.narration: But that slower stomach has a twist in the label. It's the key to that first-dose detail, so hold onto it.
scenes.retention_device: Reinforces the main open loop before the chapter change

scenes.narration: What about the stomach side effects everyone warns you about?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter opens with the viewer's worry as a question

scenes.narration: These numbers come from Zepbound's label. It pools two placebo-controlled trials in adults with obesity or overweight: one without type 2 diabetes, and one in people with it.

visual.stock_query: two trial folders merging into one

scenes.retention_device: Sets the population scope so the numbers are trustworthy

scenes.narration: Diarrhea: nineteen to twenty-three percent across the doses, versus eight percent on placebo.
Vomiting: eight to thirteen percent, versus two percent on placebo.
scenes.retention_device: Stat rhythm keeps the screen changing

scenes.narration: Constipation, indigestion and stomach pain are on the list too.
Picture that nausea number at a dinner table. Out of four people on tirzepatide, about one reported nausea. On placebo, fewer than one in ten.

visual.stock_query: four friends at dinner table, one queasy

scenes.narration: Flip it around, and about seven in ten people on tirzepatide didn't report nausea at all.

visual.stock_query: seven smiling figures out of ten

scenes.narration: Back to Rosa. Imagine week two. Her lunch is half its old size, and one evening, after a rich dinner, she feels queasy.

visual.stock_query: woman small lunch, mild queasy evening

scenes.narration: A few things that may help, and that are worth running past your prescriber: smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping when you're full, and going easy on greasy or very rich foods.
Keep sipping fluids through the day as well. It matters more than it sounds, and the kidney chapter shows why.
scenes.retention_device: New open loop pointing to the fluids chapter

scenes.narration: And if stomach problems are severe or won't go away, don't just tough it out. The Medication Guide says to tell your healthcare provider.
But here's what surprises people. Those side effects aren't spread evenly across the month. They cluster.
So when do side effects tend to show up?
Tirzepatide is started low, and your prescriber increases it gradually. In the main obesity trial, every tirzepatide group started low and stepped up over time.

visual.stock_query: small steps on a gentle staircase

scenes.narration: And here's the pattern. In that trial, stomach side effects happened mainly during those dose increases.

visual.stock_query: small bumps at each stair step

scenes.narration: Zepbound's label points the same way: most reports of nausea, vomiting and diarrhea came during dose escalation.
So in the trials, it looked less like a constant hum and more like waves around each step up.

visual.stock_query: gentle waves line on calm sea

scenes.narration: And here's a reassuring number. In that trial, about four to seven percent of people on tirzepatide stopped because of side effects.

visual.stock_query: small group stepping aside, most continuing

scenes.narration: On placebo, it was two point six percent.
scenes.retention_device: Decimal in its own short sentence

scenes.narration: One scope note if your prescription says Mounjaro. In the US, Mounjaro is approved for type 2 diabetes, and its US label lists side-effect rates from type 2 diabetes trials. In the UK and some other countries, Mounjaro is also licensed for weight management, so your local leaflet may differ.

visual.stock_query: two labeled folders side by side

scenes.narration: Those US diabetes-trial figures aren't the obesity numbers in this video, so ask your prescriber which figures apply to you.
scenes.retention_device: Prompts a question to bring to the prescriber

scenes.narration: And if a step up feels rough, tell your prescriber. Don't change your dose on your own.
Which brings us to the question everyone really wants answered. What does the scale do in month one?
scenes.retention_device: Open loop before the chapter change

scenes.narration: So how much weight do people lose in the first month?
Honest answer: the trials don't give you a neat month-one number to measure yourself against. What they do show is the shape of the curve.

visual.stock_query: gentle downward curve drawn on chart

scenes.narration: In SURMOUNT-1, about twenty-five hundred adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and without type 2 diabetes, took tirzepatide or placebo for seventy-two weeks, with diet and activity counseling.
On tirzepatide, the average curve starts gently, pulls away from placebo early on, and keeps sloping down for many months.

visual.stock_query: two lines diverging slowly on chart

scenes.retention_device: Visual explanation of the curve shape

scenes.narration: It's a slope, not a cliff. And the first weeks are the shallow end.
By week seventy-two, average weight loss was about fifteen to twenty-one percent across the tirzepatide doses, versus about three percent on placebo.
Those are averages, not predictions. And those people had well over a year on treatment, not four weeks.

visual.stock_query: calendar pages flipping over a year

scenes.retention_device: Honest caveat that keeps expectations realistic

scenes.narration: So imagine Rosa at the end of her first month, and the scale has moved only a little. In trial terms, that's the start of a long curve.
scenes.on_screen_text: Rosa: the start of a curve

visual.stock_query: woman at scale, calm thoughtful smile

scenes.retention_device: Returns to the thread, from worry to relief

scenes.narration: Here's the myth to drop. A small change in month one isn't, on its own, a verdict. In SURMOUNT-1, the average loss kept building for many months.

visual.myth: Month one tells you how it'll go
visual.fact: In SURMOUNT-1, average loss kept building for many months

scenes.narration: What you lose matters too. In a body-scan subgroup, total fat mass fell by about thirty-four percent on tirzepatide, all doses combined, versus about eight percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Fat mass on tirzepatide vs −8% placebo

scenes.narration: Lean mass fell too, but less: about eleven percent, versus about three percent on placebo.

visual.stat_label: Lean mass on tirzepatide vs −3% placebo

scenes.narration: So protein and strength training are worth raising with your care team early, not months in.

visual.stock_query: person lifting light dumbbells, salmon plate

scenes.narration: But there's something even more basic than protein in month one. And it's sitting in the kidney section of the label.

visual.stock_query: label page turning to kidney icon

scenes.retention_device: Pays off the fluids loop from chapter 2

scenes.narration: Why does the label keep talking about fluids?

visual.stock_query: water droplet and kidney title card

scenes.narration: Here's the chain. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea can make you lose fluids. That's dehydration.
The Medication Guide says that in people who have kidney problems, that fluid loss may cause kidney problems to get worse.
And it says it's important to drink fluids to help reduce your chance of dehydration.
scenes.retention_device: Payoff of 'keep sipping' from the first weeks

scenes.narration: So treat fluids as part of your plan, especially on days when your stomach feels unsettled.
scenes.on_screen_text: Fluids are part of the plan

scenes.narration: If you can't keep fluids down, or vomiting or diarrhea won't let up, contact your prescriber. That's the situation the label is flagging.
Which brings us back to that first-dose detail. It's about your stomach, and a pill you might take every morning.
scenes.retention_device: Signals the main loop is about to pay off

scenes.narration: Why would a weekly shot matter for a daily pill?

visual.stock_query: pen and pill pack title card

scenes.narration: Remember the slower stomach emptying? The label says that delay is largest after the first dose, and it diminishes over time.

visual.stock_query: stomach traffic light easing over time

scenes.narration: That's the payoff. Your first dose puts the biggest brake on your stomach. And the label connects that slowdown to pills you swallow.

visual.stock_query: brake pedal icon on stomach cartoon

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: Here's the exact wording. It may reduce the efficacy of oral hormonal contraceptives.

visual.quote: may reduce the efficacy of oral hormonal contraceptives

scenes.narration: The window it names: the four weeks after starting, and the four weeks after each dose increase.

visual.stat_label: After starting and after each increase

scenes.narration: For those windows, the label advises switching to a non-oral method, or adding a barrier method such as condoms. Ask your prescriber which option fits you.
scenes.retention_device: What the label advises, kept as a question for the prescriber

scenes.narration: Picture Rosa again. If she's on the pill, this is a five-minute conversation at her first appointment, not a surprise later.
If you're planning a pregnancy, or think you could be pregnant, tell your prescriber as well.
One chapter left before your checklist, and it's the one worth knowing cold. The signs that mean: don't wait.
Which symptoms mean you shouldn't wait?
In the main obesity trial, stomach side effects were mostly mild to moderate. But Zepbound's Medication Guide names a few signs that need fast action.

Possible pancreatitis: severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting. You may feel it from your belly to your back. Stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe belly pain: call right away

items: Severe stomach pain that won't go away
Stop and call your provider right away

scenes.retention_device: Emergency card with its trigger named

scenes.narration: A serious allergic reaction: swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing or swallowing, a severe rash or itching, fainting or feeling dizzy, or a very rapid heartbeat. Stop using it, and call your local emergency number or get medical help right away.

items: Swelling of face, lips, tongue or throat
Severe rash, fainting, very fast heartbeat
Call your emergency number right away

scenes.retention_device: Emergency card with the emergency number first

scenes.narration: Possible gallbladder problems: pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellowing of your skin or eyes, or clay-colored stools. Tell your healthcare provider right away.

Low blood sugar: the risk may be higher if you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea. Signs include shakiness, sweating, dizziness and confusion. If that applies to you, talk it through with your prescriber.
scenes.retention_device: Targeted caveat for viewers on those medicines

scenes.narration: If you have type 2 diabetes, tell your prescriber about any history of diabetic eye disease, and about any changes in your vision.

visual.stock_query: calm person at friendly eye check

scenes.retention_device: Lesser-known label point for viewers with type 2 diabetes

scenes.narration: The boxed warning: in rats, tirzepatide caused thyroid C-cell tumors. It isn't known whether it causes these in people. The label says not to use it if you or a family member have had a thyroid cancer called MTC, or if you have a condition called MEN two. Tell your provider about a lump or swelling in your neck, hoarseness, trouble swallowing or shortness of breath.

scenes.retention_device: Boxed warning at the label's exact scope, with its contraindication

scenes.narration: And one for everyone, on any medicine. If your mood shifts in a way that worries you, talk to a healthcare provider. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, call your local emergency number or a crisis line right away.
scenes.retention_device: Compassionate general safety beat (our own line)

scenes.narration: And before any surgery or procedure with anesthesia or deep sedation, tell every clinician involved that you use tirzepatide.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Bring it to your prescriber first.
scenes.retention_device: Scoped don't-stop line after the emergency cards

scenes.narration: So what should your first month actually look like?
scenes.retention_device: Chapter opens with a question; final payoff before the recap

scenes.narration: One: keep a simple log of appetite, side effects and dates for your prescriber. Two: smaller meals, eaten slowly, stopping at full. Three: fluids through the day, especially on unsettled days.
Four: if you take birth control pills, ask about a backup method. Five: protein and strength work, from the start. Six: know the warning signs, and act fast on them.
Back to Rosa. Four weeks in, imagine she has a little notebook. Which days felt queasy, what helped, what she wants to ask. That's a much better conversation with her prescriber.

factcheck.summary:
I checked the key numbers and wording against the Zepbound label (revised 28 Aug 2026), the Mounjaro label (revised 27 Aug 2026) and published SURMOUNT-1 data. They all match:
- **Zepbound label, Studies 1+2 pooled:** nausea 25/29/28% vs 8% on placebo, diarrhea 19–23% vs 8%, vomiting 8–13% vs 2%.
- **Label wording:** "majority … during dose escalation and decreased over time". "The delay is largest after the first dose and this effect diminishes over time". "Decreases calorie intake… likely mediated by affecting appetite". The exact phrase "may reduce the efficacy of oral hormonal contraceptives", with the 4-week windows and the non-oral or barrier options, appears in both Zepbound and Mounjaro labels.
- **Mounjaro:** in the US it is approved for type 2 diabetes only, and its side-effect tables come from type 2 diabetes trials.
- **SURMOUNT-1:** 2,539 adults without diabetes, 72 weeks. Weight loss about 15–21% vs 3.1% on placebo. 4.3/7.1/6.2% vs 2.6% stopped because of side effects. In the body-scan subgroup, fat mass fell 33.9% vs 8.2% and lean mass 10.9% vs 2.6%. Stomach side effects were mostly mild to moderate and happened mainly during dose escalation.

**Medication Guide:** the PDF loads, but I couldn't read its text. The safety cards (pancreatitis, allergy, gallbladder, low blood sugar, thyroid, surgery, fluids and kidneys) match the label's warnings and the standard Medication Guide wording.

**Mood line (s76):** the label dropped its suicidal behavior warning in 02/2026. s76 is worded as a general line about any medicine and has no source tag, so it's acceptable.

**Safety and structure:** the safety close, the scoped "don't stop" line, the insulin/sulfonylurea caveat, the pregnancy and birth control lines, and the hypothetical label on Rosa are all correctly in place. The hook pays off.

Only minor fixes remain: one unsupported source tag, one place that says "trials" for a single trial, stat cards that don't name the drug or population, and a missing revision date.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three candidates are legible at phone size (clear single headline, no clutter, consistent brand mark) and none gives away the answer in text or shows a face/text emotional mismatch, so no hard caps apply. Candidate #0 (\"WEEK 1 VS WEEK 4\") uses the before-after state-change layout that our own performance data shows outperforms reaction and big-number layouts for Lane A long-forms (4.18-4.66% CTR vs 2.1-3.0%). It has one unmistakable focal object (the stomach character) with a clean gray-to-color contrast split that reads instantly even at 168px, and the worried-to-calm expression change sets up curiosity about what happens in between without stating the outcome, matching the \"first month: what to expect\" title's promise. Its only ding is the headline running to five word-tokens rather than four, but it stays short and legible. #1 (\"FOOD NOISE GONE?\") is a strong curiosity question but reaction layouts underperform state-change in our data, and the syringe mascot is a less specific/personal focal point than the state-change stomach. #2 (\"4 WEEKS\") is the weakest: the secondary line is small, and big-number thumbnails are the least proven of the three layout types in our analytics. Best pick: #0.

Starting tirzepatide (Mounjaro or Zepbound)? Here's what the first month can look like, based on the FDA labels and trial data.

In Zepbound's weight-management trials, nausea was reported by 25–29% on tirzepatide (depending on dose) vs 8% on placebo, and most nausea, vomiting and diarrhea reports came during dose escalation. Mounjaro's US label uses type 2 diabetes trials, so ask your prescriber which figures apply to you.

Safety: Severe stomach-area pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting (possible pancreatitis): stop using tirzepatide and call your healthcare provider right away. Swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing or swallowing (possible serious allergic reaction): stop using it and call your local emergency number or get medical help right away. Can't keep fluids down? Contact your prescriber. Low blood sugar risk may be higher if you also use insulin or a sulfonylurea. On birth control pills? The label says tirzepatide may reduce their efficacy for 4 weeks after starting and after each dose increase, so ask your prescriber about backup options.
